title: IoT and OT Hacking

objectives.text: Describe IoT communication patterns and name the ports and roles of MQTT, CoAP, UPnP and the main IoT radios (Zigbee on 802.15.4, BLE, LoRaWAN, Z-Wave)
List the OWASP IoT Top 10 (2018) in order and match a finding (hardcoded password, open Telnet, unsigned update, open UART) to its category
Recognize IoT threat classes (botnet DDoS, jamming, replay, Sybil, side-channel, firmware tampering) by what defenders see, and explain the Mirai case
Match IoT tools (Shodan, Nmap NSE, binwalk, HackRF, RTL-SDR, KillerBee, Ubertooth, JTAGulator) to their purpose and read their key output lines
Apply NISTIR 8259/8259A, ETSI EN 303 645, MUD (RFC 8520) and network isolation to secure IoT devices
Place OT components (PLC, RTU, HMI, historian, SIS) on the Purdue model and explain why OT ranks safety and availability first
Identify OT protocols by port (Modbus 502, DNP3 20000, S7 102, BACnet 47808, EtherNet/IP 44818, IEC-104 2404, OPC UA 4840) and explain their security weaknesses
Summarize Stuxnet, the 2015 Ukraine attack, Industroyer and Triton: target, technique class and lesson for defenders
Recognize OT discovery output and ATT&CK for ICS technique names, and explain why passive monitoring is preferred in OT
Design OT defenses with NIST SP 800-82r3 and ISA/IEC 62443 zones, conduits and security levels, data diodes and CISA's primary OT mitigations

readingMap.why: Protocol ports, the OWASP IoT Top 10 order and the Mirai case are frequent recall and scenario questions.
Learn the five phase names and what each tool is for in one line; skip tool screenshots and walkthroughs.
Default passwords, updates and isolation answer most IoT defense questions; know the NIST and ETSI baselines by name.
Purdue levels, OT protocol ports and the famous incidents (Stuxnet, Triton, Industroyer) carry most OT questions.
Recognize ICS discovery tools and output and why active scanning is risky in OT; the phases mirror the IoT ones.
Segmentation, IEC 62443 zones and conduits, data diodes and NIST SP 800-82r3 are classic defense questions.

labs.name: Analyze the OWASP IoTGoat firmware
labs.skill: Using binwalk on a deliberately vulnerable firmware image to find hardcoded credentials and insecure services, mapped to the OWASP IoT Top 10

labs.name: Run and lock down a local Mosquitto broker
labs.skill: On your own machine: see what an anonymous client can read, then enable password files, ACLs and TLS on 8883

labs.name: Inspect ICS protocol captures with Malcolm
labs.skill: Recognizing Modbus, DNP3 and S7comm traffic in public sample captures and spotting writes from unexpected hosts

labs.name: Self-assess an OT network design with CISA CSET
labs.skill: Answering a standards-based questionnaire (for example IEC 62443 or NIST SP 800-82) for a small fictional plant and reading the gap report

feynmanPrompts: Explain to a friend why a cheap smart camera can help take down a big website, and the three things the manufacturer and the owner should have done to prevent it.
Explain the Purdue model to a new plant engineer, and why the business network should never talk straight to a PLC.
Tell the story of Stuxnet or Triton in plain words: what was targeted, how operators were fooled or the safety system was touched, and which defenses would have helped.
